title: Fast Loading, Caching, and Web Vitals
summary: See what blocks the first paint, tell the browser what matters, compress and cache files the right way, and measure speed with Core Web Vitals.
intro: A page that takes five seconds to show up on a phone loses people before they see a thing, and the cause is rarely one big problem. It's the order files arrive in: a font found too late, a script that makes everything wait, or a file downloaded again when the browser already had it. This lesson follows a page load from the browser's side. First, what has to arrive before anything can paint, and how to tell the browser what matters most. Then how servers send files small and how browsers keep copies, so a second visit costs almost nothing. Last, how to measure it all, with DevTools and with the three numbers that speed tools use to judge a page, so you can tell a real fix from a guess.

steps.title: What the first paint waits for
steps.body:
A page that shows nothing for three seconds feels broken, even if everything arrives in the fourth. Before the browser can paint its first pixel, some files have to arrive and others don't. Knowing which is which tells you what to cut, what to move, and what to load later.

## The critical rendering path

Recall the pipeline from the rendering lesson: the browser turns the HTML into the DOM and the CSS into the CSSOM, combines them, works out the layout, and paints. It can't paint until it has both trees. The steps, and the files they need, between the first byte of HTML and the first paint are called the **critical rendering path**. On most pages, the files on it are:

- The HTML itself, or at least its first part.
- Every stylesheet linked in the `<head>`.
- Every classic script in the `<head>`, meaning one without `defer`, `async`, or `type="module"`.
- Web fonts, for the text that uses them, as the CSS lessons showed.

Everything else, like images, deferred scripts, and a stylesheet for printing, can arrive after the first paint.

## Two kinds of blocking

CSS is render-blocking, as the lesson on how a browser draws a page showed. The browser keeps reading the HTML while a stylesheet downloads, but it won't paint until every stylesheet in the head has arrived, so one slow stylesheet holds back the whole screen.

A classic script is **parser-blocking**. When the parser reaches `<script src="app.js">`, it stops, downloads the file, runs it, and only then reads the next line of HTML, since the script might change what comes next. The script also waits for the stylesheets above it, in case it asks for a style. As the JavaScript lessons showed, `defer` and `type="module"` scripts download while parsing goes on and run after it, so they block neither.

Look at the `index.html` Vite built in the last lesson: its stylesheet `<link>` and its `<script type="module">` both sit in the head. The stylesheet blocks rendering, since the page needs its styles. The script blocks nothing, so putting it in the head just lets its download start early.

The **preload scanner** from the rendering lesson softens both kinds of blocking: while the parser is stuck, a second reader skims ahead and starts downloading the files it sees. It only finds what's written in the HTML, though. A font named inside a CSS file, or an image that JavaScript adds, is found much later.

## Three moments with names

You'll see these in every speed tool:

- **Time to first byte**, or TTFB, from the HTTP lessons: when the first byte of the HTML arrives.
- **First Contentful Paint**, or FCP: when the first text or image appears.
- **Largest Contentful Paint**, or LCP: when the biggest thing on the screen, usually a large image or the main heading, finishes painting. It's when the page looks loaded to a person.

```diagram loading-and-caching-first-paint
Nothing paints until the stylesheet and the blocking script are done.
```

In the diagram, the HTML starts arriving at step 1. The parser finds a stylesheet and a classic script, and nothing can paint until the stylesheet arrives (step 2) and the script has run (step 3). FCP comes at step 4, when the heading paints. The big image was found late and downloaded at low priority, so it lands last, at step 5, which is LCP.

## Priorities

The browser doesn't ask for everything with the same urgency. It gives each request a **priority**, from Highest to Lowest, from what the file is and where it sits. The HTML and the stylesheets in the head get the top. Scripts in the head come next. Images start low and get raised once layout shows they're on screen, and `async` and `defer` scripts sit near the bottom. On a slow connection, files with high priority take the bandwidth first. The next part shows how to change a priority when the browser guesses wrong.

The last part of this lesson shows how to watch all of this happen in DevTools.

examples.title: What blocks in a head, and what doesn't
examples.prompt: The head of a page that loads six files. Each one is loaded a different way, and each way affects the first paint differently.
examples.code:
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Notes</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/style.css">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/print.css" media="print">
  <script src="/analytics.js"></script>
  <script src="/app.js" defer></script>
  <script type="module" src="/main.js"></script>
  <script src="/chat-widget.js" async></script>
</head>
examples.explanation: `style.css` is render-blocking: nothing paints until it arrives. `print.css` has `media="print"`, so it only applies when someone prints the page. The browser still downloads it, but at low priority and without holding up the screen. `analytics.js` is a classic script, so the parser stops at that line until it has downloaded and run, and the rest of the head waits behind it. That one line is the slowest thing here, and the usual fixes are to add `defer` or `async`, or to move it to the end of the body. `app.js` has `defer` and `main.js` is a module, so both download while parsing goes on and run in order once the HTML is read. `chat-widget.js` has `async`: it downloads in the background and runs the moment it arrives, in no particular order, which suits a script that doesn't depend on anything else on the page.

steps.title: Loading the rest on purpose
steps.body:
The browser's guesses are good, but it only knows what the HTML tells it. You know more: which image is the big one at the top, which font every heading uses, where the reader goes next, and which script can wait. A few tags and attributes pass that knowledge on.

## Hints in the head

A **resource hint** is a `<link>` in the head that tells the browser about a file, or a server, before it would find them itself.

- `rel="preload"` says: download this now, at high priority, because the page needs it soon. Use it for files the preload scanner can't see, like a font named inside a CSS file, or a big image set as a CSS background. Its `as` attribute says what kind of file it is, so the browser can give it the right priority. A preload the page doesn't use within a few seconds earns a warning in the console. And preloading a lot defeats the point: when everything is urgent, nothing is.
- `rel="preconnect"` says: open a connection to this other origin now. Recall from the HTTP lessons that a new HTTPS connection costs a DNS lookup and two round trips before the first request can go. If your fonts or images come from another origin, preconnecting does that work while the HTML is still arriving. `rel="dns-prefetch"` does only the lookup, which is cheaper when you're less sure you'll need it.
- `rel="prefetch"` says: the next page will probably need this, so fetch it at the lowest priority when the network is idle. The browser keeps it in its cache, and the next page starts faster.
- `rel="modulepreload"` is preload for JavaScript modules: it downloads a module early and gets it ready to run. Vite adds these to your built page for you.

## fetchpriority and lazy loading

The HTML lessons showed two attributes for images. `fetchpriority="high"` on the LCP image raises it from the low priority images start with, so it downloads alongside the stylesheets instead of after them. `loading="lazy"` on images further down the page, and on iframes, the frames that show another page inside yours, like an embedded map or video, waits until the reader scrolls near them, so they don't compete with what's on screen. Never lazy-load the LCP image: it would wait for layout before it even starts.

`fetchpriority` works on a preload `<link>` and on a `<script>` too, and `fetch()` takes a `priority` option, so you can also turn down something the browser would rush, like a request whose answer only matters later.

## Critical CSS and fonts

Stylesheets block the first paint, so the less CSS stands in the way, the sooner the screen fills. Some sites put the few rules the top of the page needs, called **critical CSS**, straight into a `<style>` tag in the head, and load the full stylesheet the normal way. It helps most on pages where the first paint is everything, like a news story, and it's fiddly to keep right by hand, so it's usually left to a build tool.

Fonts are the other usual blocker. From the CSS lessons: serve woff2 files, use `font-display: swap` so text shows at once in a fallback font, and preload only the one or two font files the top of the page uses. Serving fonts from your own origin also saves a connection.

## What third-party scripts cost

A **third-party script** is code you load from someone else's server: analytics, ads, chat widgets, video players, and tools for testing two versions of a page. Each one is a single line of HTML, and each one costs more than it looks:

- Another origin means another connection: a DNS lookup and two round trips.
- It runs on the main thread, the one line of work from the lesson on how a browser draws a page, where your own JavaScript runs and the page is laid out and painted, so a heavy one makes clicks and scrolling slow.
- It often loads more scripts of its own, which you don't control.
- As a classic script in the head, it blocks parsing, and if its server is slow or down, your page waits for it.
- It can read everything on your page, which makes it a privacy and security risk too.

Load what you must with `async` or `defer`, load what can wait after the page is up, and ask whether you need it at all. Teams that measure often find their own code isn't the slowest thing on the page.

examples.title: A page that loads on purpose
examples.prompt: The Trail Guide site's home page. The big photo at the top is the LCP, the font comes from another origin, and a chat widget can wait. Every hint is placed for a reason.
examples.code:
Find your next trail

Popular this week
examples.explanation: The preconnect opens a connection to the font server while the HTML is still arriving, and the preload starts the font file right away, instead of waiting until `style.css` arrives and names it. Both carry `crossorigin` because browsers always fetch fonts in **CORS mode**: with an `Origin` header and under the CORS rules from the fetch lesson, as if every font came from another origin. A font preload without `crossorigin` is fetched the ordinary way, so it doesn't match the font request that comes later, and the browser downloads the font a second time. The prefetch fetches the trails page when the network is idle, since most visitors go there next. The chat widget is `async`, so it never blocks parsing. The hero photo has `fetchpriority="high"` because it's the LCP, and the map lower down is `loading="lazy"`. Both images have `width` and `height`, so the browser saves their space before they arrive and nothing jumps.

steps.title: Caching and compression
steps.body:
The fastest request is the one the browser never makes, and the next fastest is a small one. Servers make files small with compression, and browsers and CDNs keep copies with caching. Get the two right, and a repeat visit downloads almost nothing.

## Compression

Text shrinks a lot, because code repeats itself: the same words, tags, and names over and over. A server can **compress** a file, writing it in a shorter coded form, and the browser decodes it as it arrives. The browser lists the codings it understands in an `Accept-Encoding` request header, and the server names the one it used in `Content-Encoding`.

- **gzip** is the old standard, and everything understands it.
- **Brotli**, written `br` in headers, is newer and usually smaller. One of vite.dev's script files is 1,349 bytes as it is, 750 with gzip, and 698 with Brotli.
- **Zstandard**, written `zstd`, is newer still, and some browsers accept it already.

Vite's build prints a gzip size next to each file for this reason: it's close to what really travels.

Compression is the server's job, usually one setting, and hosts turn it on for you. It's for text: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON, and SVG. JPEG, PNG, AVIF, and woff2 files are compressed already, and squeezing them again saves nothing.

## Caching with Cache-Control

From the HTTP lessons, the browser keeps copies of files in its cache, and the `Cache-Control` response header says for how long. With the hashed file names from the last lesson, two rules cover a whole Vite site:

- **The hashed files** in `dist/assets` get `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable`: keep this for a year, and don't even ask about it. That's safe because a changed file gets a new name, so the old name will never have different contents.
- **index.html** gets `Cache-Control: no-cache`. Despite its name, that does let the browser keep a copy, but it has to check with the server before each use. `index.html` can't have a hash in its name, since its address is the one people visit, and it's the file that points at the newest hashed names. Checking it every time is what makes a new version of the site show up at once.

## ETag and 304

Checking is cheap. With each file, the server sends an **ETag**, a label for that version of the file. Next time, the browser sends the label back in an `If-None-Match` header. If the file hasn't changed, the server answers `304 Not Modified` with no body, the same 304 you saw Python's server send in the first lessons, and the browser uses its copy. A `Last-Modified` date, sent back as `If-Modified-Since`, works the same way.

```diagram loading-and-caching-repeat-visit
A repeat visit checks index.html and takes everything else from the cache.
```

On the first visit in the diagram, everything downloads. On the repeat visit, `index.html` costs one small round trip that ends in a 304, and the hashed files come straight from the browser's cache, without a request at all.

## CDNs

A **CDN**, a content delivery network, is a company with servers in hundreds of cities that keep copies of your files, like Fastly, from the lesson on how the browser reaches a server. Your site's name points at the CDN, and each visitor gets the files from a server nearby, so every round trip is short. CDN servers follow the same `Cache-Control` headers, and most hosts for static sites put one in front of every site they serve.

examples.title: How a real Vite site is cached
examples.prompt: vite.dev is built with a Vite-based tool. On a Mac or Linux, ask for its home page and then one of its hashed scripts, sending the same `Accept-Encoding` a browser sends, and keep three headers.
examples.code:
curl -sI -H "Accept-Encoding: br, gzip" https://vite.dev/ | grep -iE "^(HTTP|cache-control|content-encoding|etag)"
curl -sI -H "Accept-Encoding: br, gzip" https://vite.dev/assets/app.CtbPVvaT.js | grep -iE "^(HTTP|cache-control|content-encoding|etag)"
examples.output:
HTTP/2 200
cache-control: public,max-age=0,must-revalidate
content-encoding: br
etag: W/"cef18eab92e87770ec4064eb1c38fd0c-ssl"

HTTP/2 200
cache-control: max-age=31536000,immutable
content-encoding: br
etag: W/"43ccf03468645221c34209d94ceca463-ssl"
examples.explanation: The home page says `max-age=0,must-revalidate`: a copy is stale at once and must be checked before each use, which is `no-cache` in other words. The script, with a hash in its name, says `max-age=31536000,immutable`: keep it a year and never check. Both came back Brotli-compressed, `content-encoding: br`, because curl said it could read Brotli, the way browsers do. Both carry an ETag for checking later. The `W/` in front marks a weak ETag: it promises the same content, not byte for byte the same file, which lets a server use one label for a file's compressed and plain copies. The site rebuilds often, so by the time you run this, the script will have a new name and the second command will get a 404. Open the home page's source to find the current one.

examples.title: Checking a copy with If-None-Match
examples.prompt: Send vite.dev's home page ETag back, the way a browser does on a repeat visit. Use the ETag your first command printed, since it changes each time the site does.
examples.code: curl -sI -H "Accept-Encoding: br, gzip" -H 'If-None-Match: W/"cef18eab92e87770ec4064eb1c38fd0c-ssl"' https://vite.dev/ | grep -iE "^(HTTP|cache-control|etag)"
examples.explanation: The server compared the label with the current version, found they match, and answered `304 Not Modified`, with no body at all. For a browser, that means the copy it has is still right, so it uses that one, and the whole check cost one small round trip instead of a download. Change one letter of the ETag and run it again, and you get a `200` with the page, since the label no longer matches. This is the repeat visit from the diagram: `index.html` is checked every time and almost always answered with a 304, while the hashed files are never asked about at all.

steps.title: Measuring speed
steps.body:
Guessing at speed goes wrong both ways: you fix what isn't slow and miss what is. Your laptop on fast Wi-Fi is the worst place to judge from, since most of your visitors have a slower phone and a weaker signal. So measure, on purpose, the way they load the page.

## Slowing your browser down

The Network panel can show each request's priority: right-click any column heading and turn on **Priority**. Its throttling menu, which says No throttling until you change it, slows every request down. Pick **Slow 4G** to feel what a phone on a weak signal feels. Tick **Disable cache** to see a first visit, since otherwise the browser uses the copies it kept.

## The Performance panel

The Performance panel, from the lesson on how a browser draws a page, records everything the browser does. Press its reload button, and it loads the page again and draws the load on a timeline. One track shows the network, with a bar for each request. Another shows the main thread from the second part, where your JavaScript runs and the page is laid out and painted. FCP and LCP are marked on it. Next to the timeline, Chrome lists insights about what it found, like which requests blocked rendering and what the LCP element was waiting for. The panel can slow the processor down too, by four times or more, since a cheap phone runs JavaScript far more slowly than a laptop.

## Core Web Vitals

**Core Web Vitals** are three numbers, defined by Google and reported by every speed tool, that describe how a page feels to the people using it:

| Vital | What it measures | Good |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LCP, Largest Contentful Paint | loading: when the main content appears | 2.5 seconds or less |
| INP, Interaction to Next Paint | responding: how long after a click or a key press the screen changes | 200 ms or less |
| CLS, Cumulative Layout Shift | staying still: how much things jump around while the page loads | 0.1 or less |

A page passes when three visits out of four meet the good number, so a few slow visits don't fail it, but a slow phone that many visitors use does. Each one has its usual suspects:

- **LCP** depends on the critical path from the first part: a slow server, files that block rendering, and a big image found late or downloaded at low priority.
- **INP** suffers when long JavaScript tasks hold up the main thread, as the event loop part of the JavaScript lessons showed. A click can't be answered until the task in progress ends.
- **CLS** comes from images and videos without `width` and `height`, fonts that swap in late at a different size, and banners pushed in at the top after the page has drawn.

## Measuring in code

The browser reports these moments to JavaScript through `PerformanceObserver`: you say which kind of entry you want, and it calls your function with each one (example 1). Sites use it to send the numbers from real visits to their own servers. Getting every detail right is fiddly, so most teams use `web-vitals`, a small package from Google's Chrome team that measures all three.

## Lighthouse, lab and field

**Lighthouse**, a tab in DevTools, loads your page in a set way, like a middling phone on a slow network, and scores it from 0 to 100, with a list of what to fix. That's **lab data**: the same test every time, which makes it good for catching a problem before it ships. Nobody clicks during a lab test, so Lighthouse can't measure INP. It reports **Total Blocking Time** instead: how long the main thread was too busy to answer a click while the page loaded.

**Field data** comes from real visits, on real phones and networks. You collect it with your own code, and for popular sites, Chrome collects it too, from people who agreed to share it, and publishes it as the **Chrome UX Report**. Search engines use those numbers as one of the signals for ranking pages. The lab tells you what to fix, and the field tells you whether people noticed.

That's the last part of shipping your code. The next lesson looks at the libraries and frameworks teams build on top of it all.

examples.title: Watching for the LCP
examples.prompt: A simple trail page: a heading, a paragraph, and a big photo. Load it with the network throttled to a slow connection, then paste this into the Console. `buffered: true` asks for entries from before the code ran.
examples.output:
LCP candidate at 176 ms:

, 10450 pixels LCP candidate at 1708 ms: , 720000 pixels
examples.explanation: The browser reports a new candidate each time something bigger than the last one paints. The heading painted first, at 176 ms, and was the largest thing on screen at that moment. The photo arrived about a second and a half later and took over, with 720,000 pixels, its 1,200 by 600. The last candidate before the reader clicks or scrolls is the page's LCP, so this page's LCP is 1.7 seconds: inside the good line, on a slow connection. `startTime` counts from when the page started loading. Run the same thing with no throttling, on localhost, and it printed a single line, the photo at 32 ms, since the photo arrived before the first paint. Your numbers will differ.

recap:
- The first paint waits for the HTML, the stylesheets in the head, and any classic scripts there, so keep that path short.
- CSS blocks rendering, classic scripts block parsing, and defer, async, and module scripts block neither.
- Preload, preconnect, prefetch, fetchpriority, and lazy loading tell the browser what matters most.
- Every third-party script costs a connection, time on the main thread, and some of your visitors' privacy.
- Servers compress text with gzip or Brotli, and the Content-Encoding header says which one they used.
- Hashed files get max-age=31536000 and immutable, and index.html gets no-cache, so it's checked and answered 304 when unchanged.
- LCP, INP, and CLS measure loading, responding, and staying still, and three visits in four should be good.
- Lighthouse tests in the lab, and field data from real visits tells you whether people noticed.
